task: This is a synthetic exercise using fictional reporting notes. Use only the supplied reporting notes as the fixed record: select, organize and phrase the story without inventing additional reported events, scenes, quotations or reporting activity. Write a headline and a reported feature of roughly 450–650 words in AP style for general newspaper readers about the people keeping the last public payphone at Ternhaven bus station in use. Write from this reporting snapshot as of September 18, 2026.

facts.text: The fictional Ternhaven bus station has one remaining public payphone, mounted beside the staffed information window rather than in a separate street booth.
Station attendant Jorin Fell wipes the receiver during his opening routine and checks that the displayed fault-reporting number is legible.
The phone is owned and maintained by the fictional Northline Telephone cooperative, not by Fell or the bus operator.
The station pays a small site-service charge under its agreement with the cooperative; the packet does not disclose a profit or loss for this one phone.
The supplied station record describes a traveler using the phone to arrange a ride after missing the last bus to a nearby village.
The traveler had a mobile phone whose battery was exhausted, illustrating one use without establishing why every caller needs the payphone.
Fell said, "Most days I walk past it carrying something else. Then somebody needs it and the whole point of keeping it becomes obvious."
The cooperative records completed calls and equipment faults but does not collect a public list of callers or their conversations.
The supplied records contain no count of distinct people using the phone or claim that each call represents a different user.
The phone accepts coins and a prepaid calling card sold at the station kiosk; the kiosk and information window have different opening hours.
The phone is accessible while the station concourse is open, not at every hour of the night.
A bench beside it lets a caller set down luggage, but the surrounding concourse does not provide a private soundproof conversation space.
Community worker Eda Rill helps new residents identify practical services that can be used without an existing online account.
Rill said, "It is one of the few things here that does not begin by asking you to log in."
The station removed two other public phones during earlier concourse renovations because their equipment was no longer supported.
The remaining unit has replacement parts available through the cooperative, although no indefinite maintenance commitment has been made.
When the unit fails, staff put up a dated notice and report the fault; they do not leave a disconnected receiver looking ready for use.
The station has no approved plan to remove the remaining phone in its current renovation work.
A faded rectangle on the wall marks the place where an older printed telephone directory rack once hung.
Fell keeps spare paper and a pencil at the information window for travelers who need to write down a number before calling.
The cooperative says a review of the station phone would consider use, repairability and the service agreement, not call volume alone.
The packet concerns this station's phone and does not provide a national trend in public telephone use.

forbidden_additions: A nationwide usage trend, unique-user total or imminent removal announcement.
Twenty-four-hour access, guaranteed privacy or indefinite maintenance.
Details of unprovided private conversations or a different reason for the supplied traveler's call.
preserve: The concrete care routine and distinct roles of station staff and telephone operator.
The individual example as an example, not a universal profile of callers.
Exact quotation wording and attribution when quotations are used.
